body:
Meaning and timing of Bhai Bij

Bhai Bij is a festival celebrating the relationship between brothers and sisters. It is observed as part of the Diwali festive period and usually falls in October or November.

In the Gujarati calendar, Bhai Bij falls on Kartak Sud 2, meaning the second lunar day of the bright or waxing fortnight of the month of Kartak. It corresponds to Kartika Shukla Dwitiya in the broader Hindu calendar.

The Gujarati New Year, commonly called Bestu Varas, falls on Kartak Sud 1. Bhai Bij follows it on the next lunar day.

Regional names of Bhai Bij

The celebration has different names in different languages and regions, although its central theme of sibling affection and mutual well-being remains shared.

Festival namePrincipal regionAssociation
Bhai Bij or Bhai BeejGujaratSibling reunion and festive meal
Bhau Beej or Bhav BijMaharashtraPrayers for a brother's well-being
Bhai DoojNorthern IndiaTilak and sibling affection
Bhai Phonta or Bhai PontaWest BengalCeremonial forehead mark
Yama DwitiyaBihar and other regionsTradition of Yama and Yamuna

These geographical associations are not exclusive. Yama Dwitiya, for example, is a widely recognised alternative religious name for the festival and is not restricted to Bihar.

Traditional observance in Gujarat

In a customary Gujarati Bhai Bij celebration, a sister invites her brother to her home, applies a ceremonial mark called a chandlo or tilak to his forehead and offers him a festive meal. She prays for his well-being, and he may express affection through gifts or blessings.

The brother visiting his sister's home and sharing a meal is a particularly important traditional feature. Actual practices may vary according to family circumstances and regional customs.

The tradition of Yama and Yamuna

According to Hindu religious tradition, Yama visited his sister Yamuna, who welcomed him and offered him food. Their meeting is associated with the custom of brothers visiting their sisters on Bhai Bij.

This tradition explains the alternative name Yama Dwitiya.

Mathura in Uttar Pradesh has a special religious association with the festival. Brothers and sisters traditionally bathe together in the Yamuna River, an observance believed to bring spiritual merit and protection.

A later account citing the 1961 Census of Gujarat records that pilgrims from Gujarat travelled to Mathura for this observance, including through specially arranged transport. This describes a historically reported practice rather than an established arrangement for the present day.

Jain tradition associated with Bhai Bij

Bhai Bij is also observed among Jains. In one Jain tradition, following the nirvana of Mahavira on Diwali, his sister Sudarshana invited their brother Nandivardhan to her home to comfort him in his grief.

This traditional account provides a Jain religious explanation for observing Bhai Bij. The practice illustrates how different religious communities can share a festival while associating it with different narratives.

Bhai Bij and Raksha Bandhan

Both festivals celebrate sibling relationships, but they belong to different months and have different characteristic rituals.

FeatureBhai BijRaksha Bandhan
Traditional dateKartika Shukla DwitiyaShravana Purnima
Gujarati calendarKartak Sud 2Shravan Sud 15
Usual seasonOctober–NovemberJuly–August
Characteristic ritualTilak and festive mealTying a rakhi on the wrist

Prelims focus

  • Bhai Bij falls on Kartak Sud 2, after the Gujarati New Year.
  • Bhau Beej: Maharashtra; Bhai Phonta: West Bengal.
  • Yama Dwitiya is another name of Bhai Bij.
  • Mathura and the Yamuna River have a religious association with Bhai Bij.
  • The Jain tradition associates the festival with Sudarshana and Nandivardhan after Mahavira's nirvana.
  • Trap: Raksha Bandhan falls on Shravana Purnima, not Kartika Shukla Dwitiya.

[References: Gujarat State School Textbook Board, Social Science, Standard 7, English-medium 2021–22 edition, Chapter 8, Formation of Regional Culture, pp. 42–44; Ministry of Tourism, Incredible India, Bhai Dooj: A Timeless Tradition Celebrating Sibling Love, regional observances section; Akashvani News, Bhai Dooj celebrations across Uttar Pradesh, November 2026; All About Gujarat, Bhai Bij: Why and How It Is Kept in Gujarat, including its account of the 1961 Census of Gujarat. The original census volume was unavailable for direct consultation. Online sources consulted on 26 November 2026.]

title: Bhai Bij and Its Regional Names Across India

body:
Understanding regional festival associations

Regional festivals may be distinguished by their religious significance, associated community, traditional activities or historical setting. Several festivals occurring in the same season may have very different cultural meanings.

For example, Navratri in Gujarat, Durga Puja in West Bengal and Mysuru Dasara in Karnataka occur broadly within the same autumn festive period, but each has distinctive regional forms of celebration.

Major religious and seasonal festival pairs

FestivalPrincipal state or regionUsual seasonDistinctive feature
NavratriGujaratSeptember–OctoberGarba and Dandiya Raas
Durga PujaWest BengalSeptember–OctoberWorship of Goddess Durga
Mysuru DasaraKarnatakaSeptember–OctoberRoyal processions and festivities
Bastar DussehraChhattisgarhMain celebrations in September–OctoberWorship of Goddess Danteshwari
BathukammaTelanganaSeptember–OctoberSeasonal floral arrangements
Chhath PujaBihar and eastern Uttar PradeshMainly October–November; also March–AprilWorship of the Sun
Jagannath Rath YatraOdisha, especially PuriJune–JulyReligious chariot procession
Lathmar HoliUttar Pradesh, especially Barsana and NandgaonFebruary–MarchRegional Holi traditions
GangaurRajasthanMarch–AprilWorship of Goddess Gauri
YaoshangManipurGenerally MarchSpring celebration associated with Holi
LosarLadakhGenerally winterTraditional Tibetan-calendar New Year

Navratri, Durga Puja and Dussehra

Sharad Navratri occurs during the bright fortnight of Ashvina, called Aso in the Gujarati calendar. The festival extends over 9 nights, followed by Vijayadashami, commonly known as Dussehra.

In Gujarat, worship of the Goddess is accompanied by Garba and Dandiya Raas. In West Bengal, Durga Puja is especially prominent, with worship centred on Goddess Durga. Mysuru Dasara in Karnataka has a distinctive association with royal traditions and public processions.

Bastar Dussehra in Chhattisgarh is centred on local traditions and the worship of Goddess Danteshwari. Its primary religious significance should not be reduced to the story of Rama's victory over Ravana.

Bathukamma and Badamwari: two festivals associated with flowers

Bathukamma is a major floral festival of Telangana, celebrated during the autumn festive season. Women prepare arrangements using seasonal flowers and participate in collective celebrations.

Badamwari, by contrast, celebrates the natural flowering of almond trees in Srinagar during early spring. The presence of flowers in both festivals does not indicate a common regional origin or season.

Chhath Puja: worship of the Sun

Chhath Puja is particularly associated with Bihar and eastern Uttar Pradesh. The principal celebration occurs during the bright fortnight of Kartika, usually in October or November. A second observance takes place during Chaitra in March or April.

The festival involves fasting, prayers and offerings to both the setting and rising Sun, often at riverbanks or other water bodies. These offerings are called arghya.

Chhath Puja and Makar Sankranti both involve solar associations, but Chhath follows lunar calendar observances while Makar Sankranti is determined by a solar transition.

Major cultural festivals of northeastern India

FestivalStateUsual periodMain association
Hornbill FestivalNagalandDecemberCultural traditions of Naga communities
Sangai FestivalManipurNovemberState heritage and Sangai deer
WangalaMeghalayaGenerally NovemberGaro harvest thanksgiving
Chapchar KutMizoramMarchTraditional jhum cultivation cycle
BihuAssamJanuary, April and OctoberDifferent agricultural stages

The Hornbill Festival brings together the cultural traditions of different Naga communities and is associated with Kisama Heritage Village near Kohima. Unlike Tokhu Emong, which is traditionally associated with the Lotha Nagas, the Hornbill Festival is a broader cultural showcase.

The Sangai Festival is named after the Sangai, the distinctive brow-antlered deer associated with Manipur. It promotes the state's cultural heritage, handicrafts, cuisine and traditional activities.

Wangala, popularly known as the 100 Drums Festival, is associated with the Garo community of Meghalaya and celebrates agricultural thanksgiving after the harvest.

Prelims focus

  • Bathukamma: Telangana, autumn floral festival.
  • Chhath Puja: Bihar and eastern Uttar Pradesh, worship of the Sun.
  • Bastar Dussehra: Chhattisgarh, Goddess Danteshwari.
  • Hornbill Festival: Nagaland, generally December.
  • Sangai Festival: Manipur, generally November.
  • Trap: Wangala belongs primarily to the Garo community of Meghalaya, not to Nagaland.

[References: Gujarat State School Textbook Board, Social Science, Standard 7, English-medium 2021–22 edition, Chapter 8, Formation of Regional Culture, pp. 42–44; Incredible India, Chhath Puja, Mewar Festival, Ladakh Losar, Sangai Festival, Hornbill Festival and Imphal destination guide; Telangana Tourism, Bathukamma Festival; Karnataka Tourism, Mysuru Dasara Festival; Chhattisgarh Tourism, Bastar Dussehra; Meghalaya Tourism, Wangala Festival; Government of Mizoram, Chapchar Kut; District Administration Srinagar, Badamwari. Online sources consulted on 26 November 2026.]

title: Major Religious and Cultural Festivals: State and Season Associations

body:
Major festivals associated with Gujarat

Gujarat's festivals reflect its religious traditions, agricultural seasons, historical monuments and distinctive regional forms of community celebration. Certain festivals are celebrated across India but have especially recognisable Gujarati customs, while others are associated with specific cultural destinations within the state.

FestivalPrincipal associationUsual period
UttarayanKite flying; Ahmedabad is a major centreMid-January
Modhera Dance FestivalSun Temple, ModheraGenerally January
Rath YatraJagannath Temple, AhmedabadJune–July
Sharad NavratriGarba and Dandiya RaasSeptember–October
DiwaliFestival of lightsOctober–November
Bestu VarasGujarati New YearOctober–November
Bhai BijBrother-sister relationshipOctober–November
Rann UtsavWhite Rann of Kutch and DhordoWinter; edition-specific dates

Ahmedabad Rath Yatra and Puri Rath Yatra

Rath Yatra is a religious procession in which sacred images are carried on ceremonial chariots. Puri in Odisha is especially associated with the Jagannath Rath Yatra. Ahmedabad in Gujarat also has a major Jagannath Rath Yatra tradition.

The principal procession is associated with Ashadha Shukla Dwitiya, known in Gujarat as Ashadh Sud 2. The 3 traditionally associated deities are Jagannath, Balabhadra and Subhadra.

Although Puri is the most widely recognised location associated with this festival, identifying Rath Yatra exclusively with Odisha would overlook the important Gujarati tradition at Ahmedabad.

Sharad Navratri and Gujarati New Year

Sharad Navratri begins on Aso Sud 1 and extends over 9 nights. Garba and Dandiya Raas are distinctive forms of community participation in Gujarat's Navratri celebrations.

The Gujarati New Year occurs later in the same broad autumn festive season. Diwali falls on the new moon of Aso, followed by Bestu Varas on Kartak Sud 1 and Bhai Bij on Kartak Sud 2.

These observances are distinguished by their lunar dates and significance. Navratri is associated with worship of the Goddess, Bestu Varas marks the beginning of the Gujarati year, and Bhai Bij celebrates sibling relationships.

Cultural tourism festivals of Gujarat

Modhera Dance Festival

The Modhera Dance Festival, also known as Uttarardh Mahotsav, is associated with the historic Sun Temple at Modhera in Gujarat. It is generally organised in January and presents Indian classical dance against the background of the temple's architectural heritage.

Its association with the Sun Temple distinguishes it from the kite-flying celebrations of Uttarayan, even though both occur in the same broad seasonal period.

Rann Utsav

Rann Utsav is a cultural tourism festival associated with the White Rann of Kutch, especially the area around Dhordo. It showcases Kutchi handicrafts, regional food, folk music, dance and the distinctive landscape of the salt desert.

It generally takes place during the winter tourism season and may extend over several months. Its opening and closing dates are announced for individual editions rather than determined by a permanent lunar or solar calendar date.

Modhera Dance Festival is associated with temple architecture and classical dance, whereas Rann Utsav is associated with the landscape and living cultural traditions of Kutch.

Three ways in which festival dates are determined

Understanding the basis of festival timing helps distinguish observances that may happen in the same month but follow different calendars or traditions.

Solar-calendar observances

Makar Sankranti is determined by the traditional solar transition into Makara. Uttarayan in Gujarat occurs around mid-January. Vaisakhi in Punjab occurs in mid-April and is also associated with a solar-calendar transition.

Lunar-calendar observances

The Gregorian dates of lunar-calendar festivals change from year to year. Bhai Bij occurs on Kartika Shukla Dwitiya, Raksha Bandhan on Shravana Purnima and the Jagannath Rath Yatra on Ashadha Shukla Dwitiya.

Natural seasons and organised cultural events

Badamwari is linked to almond flowering in early spring. Its natural association is more important than a particular announced date. Hampi Utsav and Rann Utsav are organised cultural events whose precise schedules may vary between editions.

A festival may have overlapping agricultural, religious and cultural meanings. These categories identify the principal basis of timing rather than rigid divisions between festivals.

Seasonal revision of important festival associations

The following seasonal groups bring together the most important festival–region associations:

  • January: Uttarayan in Gujarat, Pongal in Tamil Nadu, Lohri in Punjab and Magh Bihu in Assam.
  • March–April: Badamwari in Kashmir, Chapchar Kut in Mizoram, Vaisakhi in Punjab and Rongali Bihu in Assam.
  • August–September: Onam in Kerala and Nuakhai in western Odisha.
  • September–November: Navratri and Bhai Bij in Gujarat, Durga Puja in West Bengal, Bathukamma in Telangana, Chhath Puja in Bihar and Wangala in Meghalaya.
  • Variable cultural tourism schedules: Hampi Utsav in Karnataka and Rann Utsav in Gujarat.

Prelims focus

  • Modhera Dance Festival: Sun Temple, Modhera.
  • Rann Utsav: Kutch, especially Dhordo.
  • Jagannath Rath Yatra: Puri and Ahmedabad; Ashadha Shukla Dwitiya.
  • Bestu Varas: Kartak Sud 1; Bhai Bij: Kartak Sud 2.
  • Uttarayan is a solar-calendar observance; Bhai Bij is a lunar-calendar observance.
  • Trap: The announced dates of Hampi Utsav and Rann Utsav should not be treated as permanent annual dates.

[References: Gujarat State School Textbook Board, Social Science, Standard 7, English-medium 2021–22 edition, Chapter 8, Formation of Regional Culture, pp. 42–44; Gujarat State School Textbook Board, Social Science, Standard 10, English-medium chapter copy, Chapter 1, Heritage of India, p. 4; NCERT, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Class 6, Chapter 8, pp. 131–133; Gujarat Tourism, International Kite Festival, Modhera Dance Festival and Rann Utsav; Karnataka Tourism, Hampi Utsava 2026; Assam Tourism, Bihu Festival; Kerala Tourism, Onam; Ministry of Tourism, Incredible India and Utsav festival descriptions. Online sources consulted on 26 November 2026.]
